questions.q: If you flip a standard coin, what is the probability of getting "Tails"?
questions.a: The probability is 1/2 or 0.5. A student who says "it's 50/50" understands the chance but needs to learn how to represent it as a formal mathematical value (fraction/decimal).

questions.q: If you roll a standard 6-sided die, is it possible to roll an 8? What is its probability?
questions.a: It is impossible; the probability is 0. A student who answers "1/8" or "1/6" is confusing the number of faces on the die with the requested outcome.

questions.q: In a box of 10 chocolates, 3 are dark chocolate and 7 are milk chocolate. If you pick one, what is the probability of picking a dark chocolate?
questions.a: The probability is 3/10 or 0.3. A student who answers "3/7" has confused the "favourable" outcomes with the "other" outcomes, forgetting to use the total (10) as the denominator.

questions.q: Why is it impossible to have a probability of 1.5?
questions.a: Probability must be between 0 and 1 because you cannot have more favourable outcomes than there are total outcomes. A student who thinks it can be higher than 1 is misunderstanding the ratio nature of probability.

questions.q: If a teacher says there is a 0% chance of a pop quiz today, what does that mean for the students?
questions.a: It means the event is impossible; the quiz will definitely not happen. A student who thinks 0% means "a tiny bit likely" has not grasped the definition of 0 as an impossible event.

questions.q: Create a scenario where the probability of an event is 1.
questions.a: An example is: "What is the probability that the sun will rise tomorrow?" or "If a bag contains only red balls, what is the probability of picking a red ball?" A student who provides a scenario that is merely "likely" (e.g., "the probability of raining") has not understood that 1 means the event is certain.
